opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the simplest way to see it is this: we have far more dull, dirty, and dangerous work in the world than we have people willing to do it. Factories, warehouses, logistics, elder care, households — there's a huge labor gap, and it's growing as populations age. Humanoid robots are interesting precisely because the world is built for the human form. Every factory floor, every kitchen, every tool was designed around two hands and two legs. If you can build a general-purpose robot that fits into that world, you don't have to redesign the environment to deploy it. That's a massive unlock economically.

Where Groot comes in is the brain. Historically, robotics has been a one-off business: you hire a team of PhDs, spend months programming a robot to do one narrow task in one specific setting, and if anything changes — the lighting, the object, the layout — it breaks. That doesn't scale. The idea of a foundation model for robots is the same idea that worked for language: train one big model on a huge diversity of data, and it learns general skills that transfer. Then the marginal cost of teaching a robot a new task drops dramatically, maybe to a handful of demonstrations or even just a language instruction.

So I see value showing up in waves. The first wave is in structured-but-variable industrial settings — picking, packing, moving totes, machine tending — where the tasks are repetitive but the current automation is too brittle. The next wave is more open-ended environments like retail, hospitals, and eventually homes, which require much more generalization and safety.

And I'd say the deeper economic story is that robotics becomes a platform, not a bespoke project. NVIDIA's view is that we provide the full stack — the compute to train the model in the data center, the simulation to generate synthetic data at scale, and the onboard chips to run the model on the robot — so that hundreds of hardware companies can build on top of it, the way developers built on CUDA. If we get that right, the value isn't just in any one robot doing one job. It's that physical labor itself starts to look more like software: something you can scale, update, and improve continuously. That's the part I find most exciting. I think everything that moves will eventually be autonomous, and we're at the very start of that curve.

r001.rationale: It mentions teaching tasks through demonstrations or a language instruction, but does not state that arbitrary instructions for tasks a reasonable human can perform are the condition for substantial economic value.

r002.rationale: It describes technical hurdles such as brittleness and safety, but does not state that realizing the economic value also involves challenges beyond the technology itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, the first wave of economic value won't come from a humanoid folding your laundry at home. It'll come from the places where the environment is already somewhat structured and the task is repetitive but still too variable for traditional automation. Think warehouses, logistics, manufacturing lines, hospitals doing restocking and transport. These are jobs where there's a massive labor shortage right now, and where a robot that can do the task at maybe eighty percent of human speed but twenty-four hours a day already pencils out.

What changes with a foundation model like Groot is the economics of deployment. Historically, every robot application was a bespoke engineering project. You'd spend months programming one arm to pick one kind of part, and if the part changed, you'd start over. That's why robotics has been stuck in the auto factory for fifty years. With a general-purpose model, the robot comes with a broad prior about how the physical world works, how objects behave, how to grasp and manipulate, how to follow a natural language instruction. Then you fine-tune or just prompt it for the specific task. The cost of going from "I have a robot" to "the robot is doing useful work" collapses from months to days, and that's the real unlock.

The second thing is that the data flywheel starts spinning. Every robot in the field generates experience that feeds back into the model, so the hundred-thousandth deployment is dramatically cheaper and more capable than the first. That's what happened with language models and I think it's exactly what will happen in robotics.

And then longer term, I'd say the ceiling here is a bit different than with software. Physical labor is something like half of global GDP. If you can build a general physical agent, you're not just automating a workflow, you're adding capacity to the real economy. So I think about it less as "which jobs get replaced" and more as "how much more can we build and do when the physical world becomes programmable."

r001.rationale: The response says Groot can follow natural-language instructions and handle varied physical tasks, but it does not state that arbitrary instructions for tasks a reasonable human can perform are the condition for substantial economic value.

r002.rationale: The response discusses deployment economics and labor shortages, but does not identify challenges beyond the technology itself.

astra-6.text:
I think the economic value comes from giving robots the ability to do a wide range of useful physical tasks without having to engineer a separate system for every task. If you need to program every movement for every new environment, deployment becomes expensive and hard to scale. A foundation model offers a path toward robots that can learn new skills and adapt more efficiently.

The first opportunities are likely to be in settings where the work is repetitive, physically demanding, and reasonably structured—moving materials, handling parts, or supporting manufacturing. The important question is whether the robot can do that work reliably, safely, and at a cost that makes sense.

Over time, the bigger opportunity is to reuse what robots learn across tasks and environments. If each deployment helps improve the capabilities available to the next deployment, you start to reduce the cost of bringing useful physical automation to more businesses. That’s where the potential becomes really substantial.

r001.rationale: It describes robots learning and adapting across useful tasks, but does not identify carrying out arbitrary language instructions for tasks a reasonable human can perform as the condition for substantial value.

r002.rationale: It says deployment can be expensive and that the work must make sense at a viable cost, making clear that realizing economic value depends on economic and deployment considerations alongside robot capability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is to make robots useful across a much wider range of tasks. Today, a lot of the cost of automation comes from engineering a system for one particular job. If you change the task or the environment, you have to do a lot of that work again.

With a foundation model like Groot, the goal is for robots to share a common set of capabilities and then adapt to specific jobs with much less additional training. That could change the economics of deploying robots in factories, warehouses, and eventually other environments.

But the value comes from doing useful work reliably. Can the robot complete the task safely? Can it recover when something unexpected happens? How much human supervision does it need? Those are the things that determine whether a compelling demonstration becomes a productive system. I’d expect adoption to start with well-defined tasks, then expand as the capabilities and reliability improve.

r001.rationale: The response describes adapting robots to a wider range of jobs, but does not identify arbitrary language instructions for tasks a reasonable human can perform.

r002.rationale: It discusses reliability, safety, recovery, and supervision as deployment factors, but does not state that realizing the value involves challenges beyond the technology itself.
